children: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand's initial response to the COVID-19 pandemic was appropriate and effective, but monetary policy stimulus remained in place too long, an independent review found on Tuesday.

The review was undertaken at the behest of New Zealand's current government, which was not in power during the pandemic. It comes after inflation in New Zealand rose to a peak of 7.3% in the fourth quarter of 2022, forcing the central bank to hike rates to slow an overheated economy.

The review found that the initial monetary policy response was praiseworthy, rapid and, for New Zealand, innovative monetary accommodation was provided. However, it added that the Monetary Policy Committee was too slow to remove stimulus.

It found that several "guardrails" had been removed by the central bank and parliament ahead of the pandemic including a decision to introduce a dual mandate to include a focus on employment, which added scope for the committee to focus less on price stability.

The review made a series of recommendations including that the Monetary Policy Committee should adopt a more systematic strategy less reliant on discretion and more resilient to uncertainty. It also said the committee should put greater weight on real interest rates and near-term inflation signals. Another recommendation was for it to use simple policy rules and broader scenario analysis as checks on its decisions, while accounting for likely fiscal policy responses to major economic shocks.

The review also called for regular testing of tools used when interest rates are near their lower limit, more resources for Monetary Policy Committee analysis, and a review of legal provisions that could undermine monetary policy independence.

In response to the review, RBNZ Board Chair Rodger Finlay said on Tuesday that the central bank's governor and its wider team would carefully consider the report and use its insights to help inform future practice.
